background_notes.fact: For R=ℤ_(p)⊂ℚ and an R-submodule J⊂ℂ, every element of ℚ⊗_R J has the form d⁻¹⊗c with 0≠d∈R and c∈J. Multiplication is a well-defined injective ℚ-linear map with image span_ℚ(J). If J is finitely generated over R, the images of those generators span the tensor product over ℚ.

background_notes.justification: For a finite sum ∑ρ_j⊗c_j choose a common nonzero integer denominator d and integers a_j=dρ_j. Balancing gives ∑ρ_j⊗c_j=d⁻¹⊗∑a_jc_j. Multiplication is balanced because the R actions are scalar multiplication in ℂ. If its image is zero, c/d=0 in ℂ forces c=0. Its image consists precisely of rational linear combinations, and an R-generating expression for c gives the asserted finite rational spanning set.

background_notes.justification: After using that coordinate isomorphism, project each pure tensor to its component tensors. For the inverse, apply the tensor of each coordinate insertion to the corresponding tensor component and sum over finite I. The maps exist by balancing. Projection followed by insertion is the identity on the corresponding component and zero on all others; the sum of insertion-projection maps is the identity on the finite product. Checking on pure tensors therefore proves both compositions are identities. No exactness or flatness theorem is involved.

background_notes.fact: The rings R=ℤ_(p) and ℚ satisfy the strong rank condition. A finite-dimensional ℚ-vector space is free and finitely generated; finite dimension is invariant under linear isomorphism. A finite free R-module of rank n has natural finrank n, so the finite-rank uses of M001 and M002 here measure the ordinary dimensions appearing in S002.

M_R is free of the finite rank n.

background_notes.justification: A finite rational spanning set yields a basis by successively removing dependent vectors. Gaussian elimination shows an independent family in ℚ^t has size at most t, proving strong rank for ℚ and invariance of finite basis size. If an injective matrix R^s→R^t had a nonzero rational kernel vector, multiplying it by a common nonzero integer denominator would give a nonzero kernel vector in R^s. Its rational extension is thus injective, so s≤t. This proves strong rank for R; comparison of finite bases consequently identifies the rank and its natural conversion with n. Isomorphisms carry bases to bases.

background_notes.fact: In a one-dimensional ℚ-subspace of ℂ, every nonzero a spans the space, so each nonzero g has the form g=qa for a nonzero rational q. A nonzero finitely generated module has a finite nonempty generating tuple with all entries nonzero.

grounds.reason: J is nonzero and finitely generated.
Multiplication embeds QJ as the rational span of J.

background_notes.justification: The single nonzero vector a is independent over ℚ and hence is a basis in dimension one; the coordinate of a nonzero g cannot be zero. Removing zero elements from a finite generating family preserves its span, and an empty remaining family would generate only the zero module, contrary to nonzeroness.

background_notes.fact: If p is prime and q∈ℚ is nonzero, then q=p^ηu for some η∈ℤ and u with both numerator and denominator prime to p; consequently u,u⁻¹∈ℤ_(p).

grounds.reason: p is prime, in particular p≥2.
Membership in R is specified by a denominator not divisible by p.
Each q_j is a nonzero rational.

background_notes.justification: Write q=m/d with nonzero integers m,d. Repeated division by p terminates because absolute values strictly decrease when divisible, giving m=p^αm₀ and d=p^βd₀ with α,β≥0 and p dividing neither m₀ nor d₀. Set η=α−β and u=m₀/d₀. The two denominators d₀,m₀ show that u and u⁻¹ lie in R. These powers are in ℚ⊂ℂ, so even negative exponents are defined and nonzero. The finite minimum argument and the two module inclusions are already proved in S004.
